turns.learner: Hello! I want to practise finding why a text was written. I think it depends on the topic, right?
turns.tutor:
Hello! Good choice. First, a quick question: what do you think the word "purpose" means when we talk about a text?

The topic can give a clue, but it does not decide the purpose. The same topic can be written for different reasons. A text about a library can inform, persuade or complain. The writer's words show which one.

Look at these two lines about a library:
"The library opens at 9 a.m."
"Join the library today. You will love it!"

What is different in the words the writer chose?

turns.learner: The second one has exclamation mark and says join. Maybe it is just telling about the library too, both are about library.
turns.tutor:
Good noticing: the second line has an exclamation mark and the word "join". Those are exactly the parts to look at.

You are right that both lines are about the library. But the topic is only the same; the writer's words can still do different jobs.

Tell me your thinking: when a writer says "join" and ends with "!", what do you think the writer wants the reader to do?

turns.learner: Maybe it wants me to go to the library? Like an advertisement. But still I think a library text is for informing.
turns.tutor:
Yes, "Join the library today" asks the reader to do something. You noticed that from the words, not from the topic.

A library text can inform, but it is not always informing. The topic alone cannot tell us; the writer's words can.

Let's test it. Here is another library text:
"Only 5 days left! Sign up now before the library membership ends."

Which words show what the writer wants? Please quote one or two.

turns.learner: Sign up now and Only 5 days left. It makes me hurry. So this one is persuading, I think.
turns.tutor:
Yes. You quoted "Sign up now" and "Only 5 days left", and you explained that they make you hurry. That is using the writer's words, not the topic.

Now try this one on your own.

Why did the writer write this text? Give one word, such as inform, persuade, warn or complain.

"Please keep your voice low. Other readers are trying to study."

turns.learner: Hmm, voice low... maybe warn? It is in a library so I think inform.
turns.tutor:
You gave two ideas about the open text. Keep thinking about it, and I will not give the answer yet. The place where a text appears is only a clue, so look at the writer's words too.

Recap:
The topic or place does not decide the purpose.
Earlier you said "It makes me hurry", so the writer's words and what they ask the reader to do show the purpose.

Tell me the rule in your own words.

turns.learner: The words the writer uses show why he wrote it, not only the topic. Like Sign up now is persuading.
turns.tutor:
Remember: the writer's words, not only the topic, show why a text was written. Your example "Sign up now" fits well.

Now use that rule on the open text, and look at the writer's words this time.

Why did the writer write this text? Give one word, such as inform, persuade, warn or complain.

"Please keep your voice low. Other readers are trying to study."
